title: Feature-loop memory safeguards
first_prompt: There was a crash in here when experimenting with formal verification related to memory intensive tasks. This particular machine is running lightweight WSL on a small form factor laptop. We can try ru

commits.summary: Cap the feature loop's memory with a systemd scope
commits.body:
The feature loop ran as part of init.scope, the cgroup WSL shells start in, so a memory-hungry proof could exhaust the machine and take the WSL instance down. feature-loop.sh now re-executes itself in feature-loop.scope with a 4 GB cap (FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX) and no swap. It sets OOMPolicy=continue because the default stops the entire scope on the first kill, which would take claude down with the proof. It refuses to start when less memory than the cap is available or when the scope is still active.

Verified by running the real script with a stub claude on PATH under a 100M cap: the memory hog was killed with status 137, the stub survived, and the loop exited 1 through its usual no-commit path. Also checked refusal for a cap above available memory, an invalid cap and a second concurrent loop, exit 130 on systemctl stop, and that the scope unloads afterwards. A real proof run under the cap was not tested. The separate lib/ work in progress is left out of this commit.

commits.summary: Limit each JBMC run's memory and report a run that dies as no verdict
commits.body:
One regression proof, ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto, reached 5.7 GB, and nothing stopped it short of the whole machine. Each JBMC run now starts under a 3 GiB address-space limit, set with JVMCONTRACT_JBMC_MEMORY_MB, where 0 turns it off. Its raised oom_score_adj makes the kernel kill JBMC before the agent that launched it. A run that runs out of memory or is killed by a signal now reports unverifiable even if it had already printed a passing line; before, a killed run was not flagged at all.

This does not explain the last WSL crash: that session logged no OOM kills, and the VM was showing clock jumps and CPU stalls before the heavy work. The encodeInto proof now stops after about 16 seconds with 'JBMC ran out of memory', so it has no verdict yet. The README warns against --no-refine-strings, which proved a variant that deliberately differs.

Verified by the agent that wrote it, against the full working copy: 71 tests passed including 3 new ones, clippy was clean, and the encodeInto proof stopped at the limit. The tests were not rerun for this commit, which was split from uncommitted feature work; cargo check --all-targets passed on the split tree. The crosscut and quorum proofs and the feature loop end to end have not run under the limit.

commits.summary: Add regression proofs over arrays
commits.body:
jvmcontract equivalence now accepts methods with array parameters and results. The harness copies each array argument exactly as long, runs the previous version on the copies and the new one on the originals, and compares results, exceptions and what each version leaves in the arrays, element by element, with two NaN results counting as equal. The scope in --unchanged-unless may quantify over an array. A differing input is shrunk in the interpreter and reported with what each version left behind. Replay and shrinking moved out of property.rs into a shared witness module. New options are --max-array-length and --no-shrink.

Verified with javac and jbmc on the PATH: all 71 tests pass, including the regression test over arrays, and clippy is clean. Written by the unattended feature loop before the crash; committed separately after the memory limits.

commits.summary: Count only VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL as a proof
commits.body:
parse_output treated '** 0 of N failed' as verified, but a solver that runs out of memory leaves every property as ERROR, so nothing has failed and JBMC ends with VERIFICATION ERROR and exit 6. With --no-refine-strings added through a wrapper, jvmcontract printed a proof that an encoder returning k + 1 behaves as before, and exited 0. Only VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL now counts, and the memory check no longer depends on capitalisation. In default mode six memory limits gave no false proof, but only because that path also happens to print 'Out of memory'.

Verified: the k + 1 reproduction now reports 'cannot be verified' and exits 1. The Quorum, Crosscut and Mica verify.sh scripts all pass under the 3 GiB limit, with 45 checks and no missing verdicts. This commit took over the description of a concurrent session's commit, whose array work is in the previous commit.

commits.summary: Give every run its own temporary paths
commits.body:
Temporary paths were process id plus nanoseconds, and concurrent runs collided: one run read a file holding another's output, or found it deleted, so a proof could report another proof's verdict. A flaky test showed the spliced output. The single-threaded CLI was not exposed, but parallel library use and the integration tests were. Log files and the default work directories of property and regression proofs now take a counter as well.

Verified: the unit suite ran 80 times with no failures, where it failed about one run in six before, all 72 tests passed, and clippy was clean.

commits.summary: Mark the encodeInto regression proof as pending, with a way to run it
commits.body:
The regression proof of a fast path in ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto can't finish at the default bounds on this machine, and its patches had been lost with /tmp. examples/apps/mica/pending now holds both patches, a script that runs either one, what was measured, what a bounded proof doesn't say, and how to pick it up on a larger machine. It's linked from the examples index, the Mica README, the library's limits and the source comment on the memory limit.

The earlier belief that smaller arrays didn't reduce memory was wrong: lowering --unwind as well is what helps. At 3 and 6 the correct version is proved in 94 s and 600 MB, at 4 and 6 in 275 s and 664 MB, and the bug is found at 2 and 6 in 6 s. Only the default bound of 8 runs out of memory at 3 GiB.

commits.summary: Fail integration tests when a tool they need is missing
commits.body:
A test that skips passes, so a run with a broken PATH was green while proving little: javac missing skipped most of the suite in silence. A missing javac, jbmc or TLC now fails the tests that need it, naming the tool, and JVMCONTRACT_SKIP_MISSING_TOOLS=1 asks for the skip. The check that a test is running inside the repository still skips, because that isn't a broken setup.

Verified by running the suite with an empty PATH (22 tests fail, naming javac and jbmc), the same with the skip set (exit 0), with javac but no jbmc (9 tests fail, naming jbmc), and with every tool present (all pass).

commits.summary: Name overloaded targets by parameter types, and accept -2147483648
commits.body: A target may now name an overload by its parameter types, 'pkg.Class#pow(int, int)', in Java's spelling, simple or qualified. verifier::select_method does this for derive, equivalence and prove, and a bare overloaded name is refused with the list of overloads. Contract::file_name maps it to Class.pow-int-int.contract. The expression language accepts -2147483648, as Java does. Both came out of running the /verify-bytecode skill's pieces on apache/commons-numbers#223.

commits.summary: Add the /verify-bytecode Claude Code skill, as a plugin with a one-command installer
commits.body:
plugins/jvmcontract/ is a Claude Code plugin whose skill, /verify-bytecode <pull request>, fetches a GitHub pull request as its merge base and head (scripts/fetch-pr.sh), compiles one module of each with Maven or Gradle and prints its classes and dependency classpath (scripts/build.sh, with a configuration-cache-safe Gradle init script), and then has the agent pick a proof per changed method: a regression proof with jvmcontract equivalence for static methods over primitives and integral arrays, a confined-change proof with --unchanged-unless when the pull request declares a change, a property proof of the Javadoc's @throws, @return and @param claims with jvmcontract prove, a behavioural contract diff for finite-domain methods, and capability and API contract diffs for the module, always. SKILL.md is the procedure, reference.md the tool's commands, expression language, refusals and measured costs for the agent, and report-template.md the report's shape. The skill runs on model: opus (Opus 5.5) and is only invoked explicitly. install.sh installs the skill into ~/.claude/skills, builds jvmcontract with cargo install --git (installing Rust first if needed), and checks for a JDK, JBMC, gh, build tools and jq; .claude-plugin/marketplace.json at the repo root makes 'claude plugin install jvmcontract --marketplace pilifs/in-the-loop' the other one-command path. The plugin README gives the install, what it proves, and five libraries to try it on (Commons Numbers, Joda-Time, Commons Codec, jackson-core, Commons Lang); the repo README links it. The landing page for terminalvalue.net/verify-bytecode-skill/ is in the Terminal-Value repository, not here.

On a real pull request, apache/commons-numbers#223, the regression proof of pow(int, int) found the fix's input pow(k=-2, e=31) (before: ArithmeticException, after: -2147483648) in 185 s; the Javadoc property proved in 1.4 s; the MIN_VALUE property proved on head in 1.0 s and was refuted on base in 0.7 s; the confined-change proof did not finish in 300 s. The Maven build of the external project could not be run in this session (the permission classifier declined it), so the changed file was compiled with javac alone; build.sh's Gradle path was verified on examples/apps/boxoffice and its Maven path only by reading.

Verified: the new integration test an_overloaded_method_is_named_by_its_parameter_types and the expression unit tests pass; the whole suite passed except one JBMC test that failed under contention with a concurrent proof and passed alone; the Terminal-Value site builds with the new page.

commits.summary: Let the installer take the repository's default branch
commits.body: install.sh accepted only a named branch; an empty VERIFY_BYTECODE_REF now means the repository's default branch, for both the sparse clone of the skill and the cargo install of jvmcontract, which is what a local clone needs. Verified by running the installer against file:///path/to/this/repository with an empty ref into a scratch skills directory: the skill's five files arrived with the commit recorded, jvmcontract was built and installed into ~/.cargo/bin in 40 s, and every tool check passed.

commits.summary: Tighten two lines of the verify-bytecode skill
commits.body: The install hint in the preflight step now passes --locked, as the installer does, and the note on dependency changes points at the per-jar capability contracts of step 5 instead of claiming the module's own contract covers them (it stops at the module's bytecode). Text only; the suite passed on the previous commit (49 unit and 24 integration tests).

commits.summary: Record the finished confined-change proof on commons-numbers#223
commits.body: The full-domain regression proof of ArithmeticUtils.pow(int, int) with --unchanged-unless 'k == -2 && e == 31', which timed out at 300 s, was verified by JBMC in 1083.5 s with --timeout 1500: the new pow behaves as the old one on every input but the declared one. The plugin README now states that result and the skill's reference carries the measured times as budgeting guidance (finding the witness 185 s, Javadoc property 1.4 s, narrow property 1.0 s and its refutation on the old version 0.7 s, full-domain proof 1083 s). Text only; the matching sentence on the landing page is in the Terminal-Value repository.

commits.summary: Bring the bound and verdict findings into the verify-bytecode skill
commits.body:
The skill's retry advice was --max-array-length 4 --unwind 8, which didn't finish in 170 s on ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto, while 4 and 6 was proved in 275 s and 664 MB. The reference now says to lower --unwind with the array length, starting at the length plus 2, and states that only VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL counts as a proof.

Text only. This commit also records the separation of two concurrent sessions' commits: the plugin scripts moved into the skill's commit, the overload work into its own, and the test gate's README sentence to the test gate, and messages were reworded to match. The final tree was byte-identical to the one before the separation, and each separated commit passed cargo check --all-targets. The full suite was not rerun. The confined-change proof on commons-numbers#223 was checked against its logs: all three stages ended with VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL.

commits.summary: Move the redaction rules to their own file, skip checked files, and add /review-findings
commits.body:
llm-dlc/tools/redaction_rules.py now holds the rules and the engine that applies them, and ends with a stamp: a hash of the file above it and a generated date. A transcript or log older than that date counts as checked and isn't scanned again, so check, scan, review and sync leave it alone, and sync reuses its stored log. The first stamp was set directly, without a scan, because the user said every existing file has been checked by these rules. Editing the rules voids the date until sync.py stamp has rescanned everything; it refuses while findings are open. Upload still scans what it sends. Findings in files older than the stamp are no longer reported by check or review, and check says how many logs it left out.

The engine now makes one pass over each line, and a line seen in an earlier snapshot of a log isn't scanned again. sync.py review show ID prints where a finding occurs, masked. The /review-findings skill uses it to go through findings with the user and prepares the commands for them to run in their own terminal: the rule that a person records each decision is unchanged.

commits.summary: Mask values next to JSON escapes in review show
commits.body: masked_excerpt scanned raw JSON, where an escape glued to a value hides it from the rules, which read decoded strings. So review show printed a path straight after a newline escape unmasked. It now blanks escapes at any depth of quoting before it scans, and always masks the finding it was asked about. Found during the first /review-findings run; the values shown were documentation placeholders.

commits.summary: Record the first /review-findings decisions
commits.body: The user reviewed nine findings and recorded them as false positives from their own terminal: four JVMS and JLS section numbers taken for IP addresses, four documentation placeholder paths, and one home path cut off by masked output.

commits.summary: Record session traces
commits.body: Brings the published traces up to this point: conversation that came after a session's last commit, and sessions with no commit of their own.

commits.summary: Add the /add-tla-model skill, with a circuit-breaker model as its worked example
commits.body:
The jvmcontract plugin gains a second skill, /add-tla-model (plugins/jvmcontract/skills/add-tla-model): run in a Java project, it finds or extracts the decision kernel (a pure static decide(StateEnum, SealedInput) method), derives its behavioural contract from the bytecode with jvmcontract derive, generates the TLA+ operator with jvmcontract tla, writes a TLA+ model of the system around it with the invariants the user states, checks it with jvmcontract tlc, and installs spec/check.sh, which regenerates the operator and fails on a changed contract until the diff is reviewed. SKILL.md is the procedure, reference.md the kernel shape, model recipe, TLA+ gotchas and TLC output for the agent, templates/ the check.sh and README it writes into a project, scripts/find-classes.sh locates a module's compiled classes without building, scripts/install-tlc.sh downloads tla2tools.jar into ~/tools. install.sh now installs both skills and TLC (NO_TLC=1 skips it; VERIFY_BYTECODE_SKILLS picks skills); the plugin and marketplace manifests are at 0.2.0 and describe both skills; the plugin README and the repo README document the new skill.

Verified by following the procedure by hand on a kernel with no model, Crosscut's CircuitBreaker#decide: derive (44 cases, identical to the committed contract), tla (33 cases), a new model examples/apps/crosscut/spec/CircuitBreaker.tla of the component owning the breaker (window, probe cap, wait timer, generation stamps) with a dependency that goes up and down and five invariants; TLC: every invariant holds in 102 distinct states. With example 026's kernel compiled in, check.sh stops on the two changed contract rows, and after --update TLC reports ClosedOnlyAfterEveryProbe violated after 10 steps. The model is committed in the Crosscut app, wired into its verify.sh and documented in its spec README, and is the worked example in the plugin README. Along the way the model hit the TLA+ gotcha that x' = a \/ b parses as (x' = a) \/ b (TLC: successor state not completely specified), now in reference.md. find-classes.sh was tested on the plain Crosscut build, the Gradle Box Office module and a stale fake Maven layout; the check.sh template on a copy of Crosscut (unchanged kernel, changed kernel, --update); install-tlc.sh into a scratch directory, twice. The landing page in ../Terminal-Value was updated for the second skill (uncommitted there, not deployed).

commits.summary: Split examples into demo/ and real-world/, with Commons Numbers #223 as the first real-world example
commits.body: The 56 numbered examples, the four subject systems (apps/), the generator and the Java verifier (tools/), schema/ and index.json moved from examples/ to examples/demo/, and examples/real-world/ was added for pull requests to published libraries verified with the /verify-bytecode skill: a README with the verified pull requests and the table of libraries to try next (moved out of the plugin README), and commons-numbers-223/, a record of the run on apache/commons-numbers#223 (ArithmeticUtils.pow) with the witness, the four verdicts and their times as recorded on 2026-11-01, what the run did not reach (pow(long, int), the module-level diffs), how it was produced (the file compiled alone with javac because the Maven build could not run in that session), and the commands to rerun it. examples/README.md is now a short hub for the two kinds; approaches.md and setup/ stay shared. The root README, the lib README, the plugin READMEs and references, lib's tests and doc comments, and every path inside the examples (patches, example.json, result.json, SARIF, verifier output, contract headers) point at the new paths; build.py's repo root and link depth were adjusted.

commits.summary: Run the feature loop seven times on TLA examples
commits.body:
feature-loop.sh used to repeat its instruction until a cycle made no commit. It now runs a fixed number of cycles (CYCLES=7) and exits 0 after the last one, and the instruction is now to add more advanced examples showcasing verification of TLA specs. The old instruction is replaced, not queued after the new one. A cycle with no commit still stops the loop early with exit 1, before compacting. The README describes the limit.

Verified by running the real script, including its memory scope, with a stub claude in a temporary jj repo: seven commits gave seven instructions and seven compacts, all with the new text, and exit 0; no commit on the third cycle gave three instructions, two compacts and exit 1. The loop has not been run against the real session.

commits.summary: Choose the feature loop's prompt by argument
commits.body:
feature-loop.sh now takes the name of a prompt: features is the earlier instruction to add features and examples to jvmcontract, with no limit on cycles as before, and tla is the instruction to add advanced TLA examples, seven times. Each run takes exactly one name; anything else prints the usage and exits 2 before the memory scope starts. The argument is passed through the re-execution into the scope. The README shows both.

Verified by running the real script, including its memory scope, with a stub claude in a temporary jj repo: tla gave seven instructions, seven compacts and exit 0; features ran past seven cycles until a cycle made no commit at the tenth, then exit 1, with its own text; no argument, an unknown name and two names each gave exit 2 without calling claude. The loop has not been run against the real session.

commits.summary: Add four real-world examples, a fork of JBMC's JDK models for java.nio.charset, and an OutOfMemoryError for absurd arrays in the interpreter
commits.body:
examples/real-world/ gains commons-lang-1750 (ArrayUtils.reverse: the Integer.MIN_VALUE end index found for six primitive overloads and shrunk to an empty array, the change proved confined to that index on arrays of up to four, the new version proved to throw on no input), commons-lang-1585 (ArrayUtils.subarray: the index overflow found, before OutOfMemoryError and after an empty array, and the change proved confined to the overflowing inputs), jackson-core-1203 (NumberOutput.divBy1000: nothing finished in the default budgets, division against multiplication; one witness documents the non-negative precondition; module contracts unchanged) and commons-codec-43a9aa66 (Hex.toDigit restricted to ASCII: two false violations traced to JDK classes JBMC has no model of, then the new method's whole contract proved; the old one needs a model of Character.digit). The index lists them and updates the libraries to try, including why Joda-Time has no entry. The Commons Numbers record gets the rerun's regression and confined-change verdicts.

JBMC 6.11 embeds no model of the class library and jvmcontract gives it six JDK classes, so Hex's static initializer (StandardCharsets.UTF_8, CharEncoding) ended in a NullPointerException inside JBMC and every proof over Hex was an artifact. libs/java-models-library is a plain clone (gitignored, libs/README.md says how to get it) of the user's fork of diffblue/java-models-library, branch charset-models, which adds java.nio.charset.Charset, StandardCharsets and the two name exceptions; lib/jbmc-models/ holds models of the JDK's boxing caches (Integer$IntegerCache and the Long, Short and Byte ones) with an empty range, because the real Integer.valueOf reads a nested class JBMC lacks and threw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on any autoboxing. Both go on jvmcontract's --classpath until the tool ships them. The interpreter now throws OutOfMemoryError("Java heap space") for arrays over 2^24 elements instead of allocating them: replaying the subarray witness asked for new int[2147483647] and aborted the process with a 32 GiB allocation. The skill's reference no longer claims character literals, which the expression language does not have, and the lib README names the JBMC-side limit.

commits.summary: Record the /review-findings decision on a cut-off home path
commits.body: One finding in session dfa830a1, of kind other-home-dir, was a home path cut off mid-name by a fixed-width process listing, at the start of a java -cp argument. The user reviewed the real value and accepted it as a false positive in their own terminal. review reports no open findings.

commits.summary: Run the tla feature loop without a cycle limit
commits.body:
The tla prompt stopped after seven cycles while features ran until a cycle made no commit. Both now repeat instruction, commit, compact until a cycle makes no commit, so the cycle limit had no remaining use and is removed. The README and the script's header match.

Verified by running the real script, including its memory scope, with a stub claude in a temporary jj repo: tla and features each ran past seven cycles, stopped at the tenth when it made no commit with exit 1, nine compacts and their own text. No argument still gives exit 2. The loop has not been run against the real session.

commits.summary: Check liveness and refinement in TLA+ models, and two 2PC examples
commits.body:
jvmcontract tlc now checks the temporal properties a configuration lists under PROPERTIES after the invariants, and reports them as data: a liveness property under the specification's fairness conditions, an action property, or the next-state relation of an abstract specification the model instantiates (a refinement). TLC reports a violated temporal property without naming it, so when several are listed the runner checks them one at a time and names the one that fails; a liveness counterexample is reported as its finite prefix plus how it goes on forever (stuttering in the last state, or a return to an earlier step). TLC's seed and fingerprint are fixed by default, because a liveness trace, unlike an invariant's breadth-first one, otherwise differs from run to run.

The two-phase-commit model of Quorum gained fairness conditions, the property that every participant eventually decides, and a check that the protocol implements Lamport and Gray's transaction commit (new spec/TCommit.tla, instantiated on the participants' states); its vote-receiving action is quantified over a constant set so that TLC names it in traces. Example 057 makes the coordinator keep collecting on a timeout when every vote so far is yes: every invariant holds and the contract diff is the intended one, but TLC shows a five-step run after which a prepared participant holds its locks forever, a failure no invariant or deadlock check can state. Example 058 repairs it with a grace period and a second timeout, proved live and still a refinement in 936 states. Examples 020 and 021 were regenerated against the extended model with unchanged verdicts.

Verified by the crate's unit and integration tests (a new test copies the model, breaks the timeout rule in the generated operator, and expects the named liveness violation with a stuttering trace), by examples/demo/tools/build.py on 020, 021, 057 and 058, and by Quorum's verify.sh. build.py's result pages carry the violation kind and the infinite continuation, and the README, approaches and skill reference describe the new checks.

commits.summary: Model Raft leader election around the role machine, with action properties, and three examples
commits.body:
A second TLA+ model in Quorum, spec/RaftElection.tla, is built around the Raft role machine: the servers, their terms and votes, and the RPCs between them, with the role transitions generated from the behavioural contract of RoleMachine#decide (spec/RoleMachineContract.tla) and the vote rule written as VoteRule.grant without the log. An RPC is one step, the request and its reply together, which keeps the model at 610 states for three servers and three terms; a first draft with a message set exceeded half a million states and was dropped. The configuration lists two action properties, formulas of the form [][A]_v that TLC checks on every step: terms never decrease, and a leader never becomes a candidate. There is no liveness property, since Raft relies on randomized timeouts, which the model says.

Examples 059 to 061 change the role machine. 059 stops adopting a candidate's newer term on a vote request; the contract diff is three cases and the vote rule is untouched, but TLC finds a five-step run in which one server votes twice and two leaders serve one term, a bug in how two kernels compose that each kernel's contract approves. 060 folds the election timeout into one rule for every role; every invariant holds, and the action property LeadersNeverCampaign is violated by the step in which a leader resigns into a candidacy, between two states the protocol allows. 061 makes a leader step down to follower when its own timer fires, as etcd's CheckQuorum does, and is proved to keep every invariant and both action properties in 1,153 states. The existing tests pass on all three patches.

build.py now keeps a list of models per app and picks the one whose symbol is the example's subject, so an app can have several models; the prose tables moved into the model dicts. Examples 020, 029 and 042 were regenerated to confirm the lookup for the other models (their result.json gained the violationKind and forever fields added last cycle). Verified by building 059 to 061 with the expected verdicts, by the Quorum verify.sh, which now generates the role-machine operator and checks the election model, and by TLC on hand-patched operators before the examples were written. The READMEs, approaches.md, the model README, the library README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the model and action properties.

commits.summary: Check the Raft election model under three configurations: an inductive invariant and four servers under symmetry, with two examples
commits.body:
The Raft election model in examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec is now checked under three configurations, and every example of it runs all three. RaftElectionInductive.cfg uses the new invariant Inductive as TLC's initial predicate (Lamport's inductive-invariance check): from every state the invariant admits, reachable or not, every step lands in a state it admits, which proves election safety by induction for runs of any length; a counterexample is one step and names the conjunct that fails. Inductive is TypeOK, ElectionSafety, LeaderHasAMajority and five new conjuncts about tallies, votes and terms (VotesAreBound, TalliesOfATermAreDisjoint, CampaignersVoteForThemselves, TalliesHoldTheirOwnersVote, TermZeroIsQuiet); InductiveInit is the same predicate written so that TLC enumerates it with early pruning (17,470 admitted states, four seconds). RaftElectionFour.cfg checks four servers, where a candidate can hold a vote besides its own and still be short of a majority, under a symmetry set (829 states instead of 16,974). The model's Timeout now empties a tally only on VOTE_FOR_SELF, as the Java effects mean. TLC.tla joins the committed standard modules for Permutations.

jvmcontract tlc gained --config to run a specification under another configuration file (TLC's -config, made absolute). build.py lets a model list extra configurations with a label and a description; it runs them all, takes the first that fails as the example's verdict, writes all runs to result.json (schema extended with configurations) and verifier-output.txt, and renders a configurations table and the other counterexamples in the README. Examples 059 to 061 were regenerated under the three configurations with unchanged verdicts.

Example 062: a candidate that retries its election without voting for itself again. Three servers find a seven-step run in which two candidates retry into term 2 and elect each other; the inductive step finds the one step that breaks CampaignersVoteForThemselves; four servers find an eight-step run in which a vote cast in term 1 is counted in term 2. Example 063: a candidate that retries in the same term, proved safe under all three configurations, with prose on what the proof does not say: the model states no election liveness, and under that rule a split vote never ends. Both verified by build.py with the expected verdicts and passing tests; the Quorum verify.sh runs all three configurations; the Rust TLA tests pass; the READMEs, approaches.md, the library README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the configurations, inductive invariants and symmetry sets.

commits.summary: Check the Raft election model for liveness under fairness, a fourth configuration, with two new examples and 063 rechecked
commits.body:
The Raft election model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla) gains a liveness section: fairness conditions (a server whose election timer nothing resets times out, a candidate asks for the votes it lacks, a leader sends its heartbeats), two temporal properties, ALeaderIsElected (a run that stays within the term budget elects a leader, conditioned on the budget because a bounded model without a clock cannot show a leader within any number of terms) and StaleLeadersStepDown (a leader whose term the cluster has left steps down), and a new configuration RaftElectionLive.cfg that checks them. Each action now computes its next state as a record (TimeoutNext, CanvassNext, HeartbeatNext, with Step and Changes), which the fairness conditions use through explicit enabling predicates (CanTimeout, CanCanvass, CanHeartbeat); RaftElectionEnabled.cfg checks that those predicates agree with TLC's ENABLED in every reachable state. build.py lists the fourth configuration (label 'fairness'), describes the two properties, and collapses a later configuration's counterexample into one sentence when it is the same run as the headline. verify.sh runs the two new configurations; the READMEs, approaches.md and the add-tla-model reference are updated.

Why the fairness is written out: WF_vars(A) on actions that evaluate the generated role machine made TLC compute ENABLED symbolically on every step of the liveness check, which took 60 to 90 seconds on 610 states (each condition alone took a second or three; together they blew up). Written as <>[]CanA => []<><<A>>_vars with CanA a state predicate, the same check takes a second, and the agreement check (42 seconds) shows the predicates are exactly ENABLED. The property is not vacuous: the stronger property that every server eventually leads fails, so runs within the budget exist. No symmetry set in the liveness configuration, since TLC's liveness checking is unsound under one.

commits.summary: Check that the Raft kernel's exception is unreachable and the two-phase-commit invariant inductive, with three new examples
commits.body:
The Raft election model gains the invariant KernelNeverThrows: each action's next-state record now carries a throws field (whether any role-machine decision it goes through is Throws), the actions and the enabling predicates are guarded by it, and the invariant says that no timeout or RPC a reachable state allows makes the kernel throw. The IllegalStateException the Java reserves for a leader hearing a leader of its own term is thereby proved unreachable rather than assumed; the invariant is listed in all four Raft configurations, and in the inductive one it checks that Inductive implies it. The two-phase-commit model gains a second configuration, TwoPhaseCommitInductive.cfg, with an inductive invariant of four new conjuncts about the votes counted and in flight (VotesInFlightAreUncounted, DecisionMatchesThePhase, ParticipantsAgreeWithTheirVotes, CommitNeedsEveryVote); it admits 736 states against 728 reachable.

lib/src/tla.rs parses TLC's 'Invariant X is violated by the initial state:' report, which the inductive configuration produces when the invariant it starts from does not imply the one checked, as a one-state trace; build.py labels and describes such a counterexample as a starting state. Examples 066 (a leader that throws on a vote request of its own term: reachable in four steps through a split vote, and a starting state of the inductive check), 067 (a coordinator that commits after aborting once the late votes are all yes: Atomicity in nine steps, and in one step from a state the invariant admits) and 068 (a coordinator that answers late votes with its decision again: verified under both configurations) are new; 058's patch and prose now extend the inductive invariant with the GRACE phase, and 020, 021, 057 and 059 to 065 are regenerated under the new configurations with unchanged verdicts. Verified by building every example with its expected verdict, by the Quorum verify script (29 tests, all contracts and proofs, seven TLC runs including the new configuration), and by the lib's unit tests.

commits.summary: Generate the Raft vote rule into the election model as a second operator, add a logs configuration for the election restriction, with three new examples
commits.body:
The election model's vote rule used to be written by hand in TLA+, so a change to VoteRule.java changed nothing TLC checked. VoteRule.grant is now arithmetic around a finite kernel, VoteRule.decide(Ballot, VoteRequest), whose behavioural contract (40 cases) jvmcontract derives and proves against the bytecode and jvmcontract tla turns into VoteRuleContract.tla; RaftElection.tla brings it in as the instance Vote and calls Vote!Decide from Canvass with the voter's ballot and the candidate's term and log against the voter's own, as grant does. The model gains fixed logs (Logs, over the configuration's set LeftBehind, since a .cfg cannot assign a function), the invariant LeaderCompleteness, and a fifth configuration RaftElectionLogs.cfg in which one server holds the log a deposed leader left behind (461 states); the other configurations keep their state counts (610, 17,470, 829, 610). Three JBMC properties of grant cover the arithmetic the model repeats rather than generates: one vote per term, a candidate from the past refused, and the last term compared before the length.

build.py lets a model list extra generated operators (regenerated from the patched code and matched by the example's symbol), draws the state machine from the example's own symbol, and reports the violated property when a method has several, which it used to get wrong. Examples: 069, a vote rule that lets a voter switch candidates within a term, elects two leaders that hold each other's votes (ElectionSafety in five steps, TalliesOfATermAreDisjoint in the inductive step, four servers in seven); 070, a vote rule without the election restriction, elects the server left behind, lacking a committed entry (LeaderCompleteness, three steps, under the logs configuration only); 071 (B11), the log comparison with length before term, fails the third property with a witness, which the model cannot see. Example 013's patch is regenerated against the new code. Verified by examples/demo/apps/quorum/verify.sh (31 tests, contracts, eight property proofs, eight TLC runs) and by rebuilding 013, 014, 059 to 066 and 069 to 071 with the expected verdicts.

commits.summary: Report what a model-checking verdict rests on: TLC coverage read back per contract row, a vacuous label, and three new examples
commits.body:
jvmcontract tlc gains --coverage: it passes TLC -coverage and reads the statistics back against every generated operator module the specification uses, arm by arm (an arm's guard is evaluated when no earlier arm matched, so an arm was taken as often as its guard minus the next arm's, summed over the actions that evaluate the operator; invariants take no step and are not counted). The report lists, per operator, how many rows of the contract a step of the model takes and the rows none does, in the contract's own case syntax; in --json it is the coverage field. TLC's report folds a subtree whose counts are all equal, which hid every row under an action that always takes the same one (Crosscut's Finish and Fail), so generated operators now start their first arm with a conjunct TLC evaluates twice, (\A i \in {1, 2} : i = i), and all seven committed operator modules are regenerated, the Box Office one by the Python generator, which emits the same. Coverage of a run that stops at a counterexample is partial and is left out.

build.py runs every configuration with --coverage and records in result.json which rows the change altered (the contract diff before and after regeneration, reasons stripped since they are not in the model, null rows left out) and which configurations' runs take them. A verified verdict is labelled vacuous when every run finished and none from an initial state takes an altered row that decides; rows that throw are meant never to be taken and do not count, and the inductive step, which starts from admitted states rather than a run, counts separately. example.json may state expected.vacuous, which the generator checks like the verdict. Every model-checking page has a new section, what the verdict rests on: a table of rows taken per configuration, the altered rows with the runs that take them, and the rows no step takes under the primary configuration. All 23 model-checking examples are rebuilt; 068's page now shows that only four of its eight altered rows are ever taken, and 030's that its one altered row is.

Examples 072 to 074 on the Raft election model: a vote rule that refuses a repeat request (072) and a follower that leads on a late majority (074) verify under all five configurations and are reported vacuous, since atomic RPCs never ask a voter twice or count a vote late; a vote rule that throws on a term the voter has not adopted (073) has nine rows no run takes, which KernelNeverThrows turns into the theorem the change asked for. Verified by the Rust tests (53 unit, 25 integration, including one for the coverage parser), the verify scripts of Quorum, Crosscut and Mica, and the generator, which checks every rebuilt verdict and vacuity against the example's expectation.

commits.summary: Check the circuit-breaker model for liveness under fairness, a second configuration, with three new examples
commits.body:
The Crosscut circuit-breaker model, until now checked only for its invariants and only by the module's verify.sh, gains a liveness section: fairness conditions (the caller keeps calling, every permitted call completes, the clock ticks, nothing assumed of the dependency) and three temporal properties, one for each fate of the dependency: an open breaker probes again, a dependency that comes back for good is used again, a dependency that stays down gets the wait between its rounds of probes. A new configuration, CircuitBreakerLive.cfg, checks them; plain WF_vars is fast enough at 102 states. The owner in the model now applies every effect whichever event returns it: a request can start the wait, a completion can start a new metrics generation. The breaker joins build.py's models for the Crosscut app, beside the idempotent receiver, so model-checking examples can be written against it.

Three examples. 075: an open breaker that restarts its wait on each refused call keeps every invariant and fails the first property, eight steps then a tick and a refused call forever, over a dependency that came back at step six. 076: a half-open breaker that judges its probes by their failure rate, as Resilience4j does, is verified under both configurations, with coverage showing one of its three rows taken and two out of reach of two probes at a threshold of one in two. 077: a half-open breaker that starts its probes over on a failed one keeps every invariant and fails the third property, fourteen steps then a six-step cycle of failing probes and resets, half-open forever; the first two properties pass on it, which is why there are three.

Verified by building the three examples (verdicts as expected, tests pass after the patches update them), by the module's verify.sh (tests, contracts, seven property proofs, three model runs, all green), and by reading the generated pages. The Crosscut READMEs, the skill reference, the plugin README, the approaches table and the example counts are updated.

commits.summary: Check the idempotent receiver's expiry rows under a second configuration in which the record's time to live can pass, with three new examples
commits.body:
The idempotent-receiver model (examples/demo/apps/crosscut/spec/IdempotentReceiver.tla) never let the record expire, so the kernel's Expired rows were dead to it: the coverage report introduced with examples 072 to 074 listed them as never taken, and any change to them would have verified vacuously. The model now has a constant Expires and an Expire action, the sweeper asking the receiver what to do with a record whose time to live has passed, behind it. The base configuration keeps Expires = FALSE and its outright at-most-once statement; the new IdempotentReceiverExpiring.cfg sets it TRUE, and AtMostOnce counts the results since the sweeper last released the record: at most once per lifetime, which is what a time to live means. There is no clock, so the sweeper can fire at any point, the honest model of a sweeper whose clock measures age and nothing else. The replay invariant had to be restated: comparing a reply given earlier with the store now raised a false alarm on the committed kernel once the record could expire after the reply, so the receive action now records whether the replay had a response (REPLAYED or EMPTY) and the invariant forbids EMPTY.

Three new examples, built by examples/demo/tools/build.py with the receiver model's new configuration listed in its BREAKER-style entry: 078, a sweeper that releases a record in progress by its age alone (the naive form of example 029's resolution) lets a retry execute beside the first attempt, a six-step counterexample that only the expiring configuration can produce; 079, a record that expires into a tombstone which refuses late retries, a new key state and effect, verified under both configurations with three of its six changed rows taken; 080, a record that drops its expired response but keeps its key replays a response that is gone, a seven-step counterexample. Examples 029 and 030 are regenerated with the second configuration (same verdicts).

Verified by the Crosscut verify.sh (39 tests, the four contracts, seven JBMC proofs, and now four TLC runs: 168 and 308 states for the receiver, 102 and 102 for the breaker) and by building the five examples, each with its expected verdict. The Crosscut READMEs, the demo and top-level READMEs, the approaches table, the plugin README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the configuration and the lesson about invariants an environment action can undo.

commits.summary: Check the Raft role machine's stale-reply rows under a sixth configuration in which a vote reply waits on the wire, with three new examples
commits.body:
The Raft election model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla) made every RPC one step, the request and its reply together, so the role machine never saw a reply from a term older than the server's own, and its three rows for such a reply (one per role) were dead: TLC's coverage listed them as taken by no step, and a change to them would have been verified vacuously. The model now has a constant DelayedReplies and, when it is on, two actions in place of Canvass: Ask puts the voter's reply on the wire with the term it answered in, and Answer lets the candidate take it whenever the model likes, after it has timed out into a newer term, stepped down, or won. The one-step action stays for the other configurations, so their state counts are unchanged; the new RaftElectionDelayed.cfg runs three servers and two terms (20,351 states, about three seconds; three terms would be 364,236 states and no further row), and under it steps take 33 of the role machine's 36 rows. KernelNeverThrows covers the new actions.

Three examples change the rows the configuration reaches. 081 rewrites the reply rule as a switch whose default arm adopts the reply's term, so a reply from a term the candidate has left sends its term backwards: TLC reports the action property TermsNeverDecrease in five steps, under the delayed configuration alone. 082 makes such a reply throw IllegalStateException, which is the model's own one-step simplification written into the Java: KernelNeverThrows fails in four steps. 083 adds a LOG_STALE_REPLY effect on such a reply and is verified under all six configurations, with the coverage showing the three changed rows taken only under delayed replies, where the other five would have called the verdict vacuous. The thirteen earlier Raft examples are regenerated with the sixth configuration and keep their verdicts; 072 and 074 stay vacuous, since a reply on the wire neither asks a voter twice nor counts a vote late.

Verified by the Quorum verify.sh (tests, contracts, property proofs, and TLC under every configuration including the enabling-predicate check), by building the three new examples and rebuilding the thirteen earlier ones with build.py, all with the expected verdicts. The Quorum READMEs, the demo and top-level READMEs, approaches.md, the plugin README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the configuration.

commits.summary: Check the Raft paper's run-wide claims, one leader per term and one vote per server per term, with history variables under a seventh configuration, with three new examples
commits.body:
The Raft election model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla) stated election safety as a state invariant: no two servers lead one term at once. The paper's property is about the whole run, at most one leader can be elected in a given term, and so is the rule it rests on, a server votes for at most one candidate per term; a state invariant cannot see either, since a server's vote is gone the moment it moves to a newer term and a leader that has stepped down is a follower like any other. The model gained two history variables, elected (every pair of a server and a term it has led) and voted (every triple of a voter, a term and a candidate), which each step extends with the leaders and votes of the state it lands in, a constant History that switches the recording on, and the invariants AtMostOneLeaderPerTerm and AtMostOneVotePerTerm. A seventh configuration, RaftElectionHistory.cfg (three servers, three terms, History = TRUE, 4,798 states in a second), checks them; the six others set History = FALSE and keep their state counts, and build.py runs the new one last, so every older example keeps its headline. The history is left out of the inductive configuration, since the state does not determine it.

Three new examples change the role machine's row for a vote request from the server's own term. 084 has a candidate stand down for a rival of its term (as a remedy for split votes): the six state-based configurations verify it, because the candidate also drops its own tally, and the history configuration reports AtMostOneVotePerTerm in four steps, the rule the paper's argument rests on. 085 has a leader yield to a candidate of its own term: every state invariant holds, one leader after the other, and AtMostOneLeaderPerTerm fails in five steps, the leader's freed vote being the one the candidate wins with. 086 has the leader answer such a candidate with its heartbeats instead, verified under all seven configurations with the changed row taken under each. The 13 older Raft pages were rebuilt with the seventh configuration and all keep their verdicts; 059's and 065's bugs also show as double votes under the history column. Verified by the quorum verify.sh (tests, contracts, proofs, all TLC configurations and the ENABLED check, green), by build.py on the 16 Raft examples (all as expected), and by the prototype runs under /tmp/cycle11. Docs updated: the spec, quorum and demo READMEs, the top-level README and examples index (86 examples), approaches.md, the plugin README, and the add-tla-model skill reference, which gained a paragraph on history variables of the set kind.

commits.summary: Let the two-phase-commit coordinator crash and restart on a recovery rule generated from its own contract, under two more configurations, with three new examples
commits.body:
The two-phase-commit model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla) now has a coordinator that may crash and restart. A new kernel, twopc.Recovery#decide(Phase logged, Restarted), says what a restarted coordinator does with the phase it logged: presumed abort, a logged decision is sent again and no logged decision aborts. Its behavioural contract is derived like the others, and jvmcontract tla generates spec/RecoveryContract.tla, which the model brings in as an instance, its second generated operator. The model gains a MaxCrashes constant and up and crashes variables; applying a decision now logs the phase change and then either broadcasts or, while crashes remain, crashes with the broadcast lost; Crash is a crash between steps and Recover feeds the logged phase to the recovery rule and applies its decision the same way, so a restart can be cut short too. The inductive invariant's conjunct tying the broadcast to the phase is weakened to allow nothing out, and two conjuncts are added: a coordinator that is up and decided has its decision out, and the coordinator is down only after a crash, which keeps the existing configurations at their 728 and 736 states. Two configurations are added: TwoPhaseCommitCrash.cfg (two crashes, 3,448 states, the same invariants, liveness property and refinement, with the fairness condition that a crashed coordinator restarts) and TwoPhaseCommitCrashInductive.cfg (2,728 admitted states, the coordinator up or down). verify.sh runs both, and build.py lists them after the inductive one with the recovery operator under the model's operators, so older examples keep their headlines.

Examples 087 to 089 change the recovery rule. 087: a restart that aborts whatever was logged, which under crashes reverses a commit one participant has already applied, found as a ten-step run (CommitFollowsTheCoordinator) and as one step from a state the inductive invariant admits. 088: a restart with nothing to redo in a decided phase, which leaves an abort logged and unsent when the restart that logged it is cut short by a second crash, so a prepared participant waits forever: EveryParticipantDecides, a ten-step run then stuttering, with the crash-inductive configuration naming BroadcastOnceUp. 089: a restart that resumes collecting, since the tally is logged, verified under all four configurations with the changed row taken under both that have a crash. Example 058's patch, which adds a phase, was regenerated against the new model and now also teaches the recovery rule the new phase; examples 020, 021, 057, 058, 067 and 068 were rebuilt for the two new columns, all as expected, and 057's text now describes the six-step liveness counterexample TLC reports for it under the reshaped next-state relation. Verified by the quorum verify.sh (tests, contracts, proofs, all eleven TLC runs green) and by build.py on the nine examples. Docs: the spec, quorum, demo, root, examples and plugin READMEs, approaches.md, and the add-tla-model skill reference, which gains a paragraph on modelling a crash of a part that logs its state.

commits.summary: Hold the Java two-phase-commit nodes to the model by trace validation under a fifth configuration, with three new examples
commits.body: The quorum module gained the glue around the two-phase-commit rules, written as a real coordinator is: CoordinatorNode (counts votes, asks Coordinator#decide and Recovery#decide, writes a CoordinatorLog before it broadcasts on a Network), ParticipantNode, and a Faults injector that crashes the coordinator after any I/O operation. A test-side Traces class runs them through eight scripted scenarios, four with crashes, records the state after each step in the model's variables and prints it as TwoPhaseCommitTraces.tla. The new TwoPhaseCommitTrace.tla extends the model, walks each recorded run and checks every step against the model's next-state relation as the action property EveryStepIsOneOfTheModel, plus that each run starts in the initial state; TwoPhaseCommitTrace.cfg is the two-phase-commit model's fifth configuration. build.py lets a configuration name its own spec, a trace writer run on the patched classes, and whether it counts coverage (TLC attributes none to an action property), renders a recorded run's first step with its scenario name, and matches an example's symbol against the glue methods a model lists as traced. Examples 090 to 092: a node that broadcasts before it logs (caught four steps into the run in which the timer's abort is logged and the coordinator crashes: the decision is out, the log still says collecting), a node that logs the tally only with a decision (caught at the crash that takes the counted vote with it, where the model's Crash keeps the tally), and a participant that votes no when it gives up, verified with every recorded step one of the model's. Two model changes came out of it: Perform now lets a crash fall in any step after what the step logged (a restart with nothing to do, cut short by a crash, is one recorded step; the reachable states and the four state counts are unchanged), and the coordinator's fairness conditions name the completing step (WF_vars(A /\ up')), since weak fairness of a timeout that decides nothing would otherwise force a crash and hide 057's liveness bug under crashes. Examples 020, 021, 057, 058, 067, 068, 087, 088 and 089 were rebuilt for the fifth column, all with their verdicts; 088's counterexample under crashes is now nine steps rather than ten, since counting a vote and crashing fuse into one step, and its text follows the new trace. Verified by the quorum verify script (27 checks green, 40 tests), by build.py on the twelve two-phase-commit examples with every verdict as expected, and by the result schema. Docs: the spec README, the quorum and demo READMEs, approaches.md, the plugin README and the add-tla-model skill reference.

commits.summary: Let the two-phase-commit participants crash and restart on a rule generated from their own contract, under two more configurations, with three new examples
commits.body:
The two-phase-commit model's participants now run on a third generated operator, Participant#decide (Participant.decide.contract, ParticipantContract.tla): what a participant does when asked to prepare, when it gives up, when it reads the decision, and when it restarts after a crash. The committed rule has a prepared participant hold its locks through a restart, since it cannot decide alone (the blocking property), and one that had not voted abort, since it logs its state before sending its vote. ParticipantNode is now glue around that rule, with a ParticipantLog and its own fault injector (Faults takes a process name; Network.send reports to the sender's). The model gained a constant MaxParticipantCrashes, the variables pup and pcrashes, an Act operator through which every participant action logs then sends and may crash after the log write with the vote lost or not, ParticipantCrash and ParticipantRecover actions, fairness for restarts, and two inductive conjuncts; the five existing configurations set the new budget to zero and keep their state counts, and two new ones, TwoPhaseCommitParticipantCrash.cfg (12,754 states) and TwoPhaseCommitParticipantCrashInductive.cfg (18,636 admitted states), check every run and the inductive step with crashes of either process. The trace writer records the two new variables and runs three more scenarios with participant crashes (eleven in all, 103 recorded states).

Examples 093 to 095: a participant that releases its locks on restart aborts a transaction the coordinator committed on its yes vote, found in eight steps under participant crashes and as one step from an admitted state; a participant node that sends its vote before logging it is caught only by its recorded run, at the step where the vote is out and the log still says working; a restarted participant that votes no rather than wait for the coordinator's timer is proved safe and live under all seven configurations, with the changed row taken. Example 092 was regenerated as a change to the participant's rule, 058's patch against the changed model, and 089 to 091's texts for the seven configurations; the liveness counterexamples of 057 and 088 come out in a different order under the added fairness condition, and their texts follow. Verified by the quorum verify script (30 checks, 47 tests, exit 0), by building the three new examples and rebuilding the twelve older two-phase-commit ones, all with the expected verdicts and the older headline traces unchanged except 057 and 088 as described. The build tool's model entry, the spec and app READMEs, the demo and root READMEs, the approaches table, the plugin README and the add-tla-model reference are updated.

commits.summary: Model Raft log replication with the follower's append rule and the leader's commit rule as two more generated operators, under two configurations, with three new examples
commits.body:
A third TLA+ model of the Quorum library, spec/RaftReplication.tla, has the Raft logs live where the election model keeps them fixed: leaders append entries on client requests, send a follower one entry per RPC with the entry before it and the leader's commit index, followers take or refuse them, and leaders mark entries committed. Two new Java kernels decide the two sides, raft.AppendRule#decide (the consistency check, the append in place of what the follower held, and the commit index following the leader's; 36 contract cases) and raft.CommitRule#decide (a majority holds the entry and it is from the leader's own term; 21 cases, with an IllegalStateException for an entry from a later term that the model proves unreachable). Their contracts are generated with jvmcontract update and their TLA+ operators with jvmcontract tla, brought into the model as the instances Entries (Append is a Sequences operator) and Commit, beside the role machine and the vote rule the election model already generates. The model checks the paper's log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety as invariants and, as action properties, that no committed entry is ever overwritten, that a leader's log only grows and that terms never decrease. RaftReplication.cfg has three servers, three terms and two entries under a symmetry set (19,338 states, four seconds), the smallest model in which two logs can share an entry over different histories; RaftReplicationFigureEight.cfg has four terms and one entry per leader (8,838 states), the budget of figure 8 of the paper, which three terms cannot show.

Three examples: 096 relaxes the consistency check to the previous index existing, and TLC finds in twelve steps two logs that share an entry of term 3 over different entries at index 1, with the figure 8 configuration finding a follower that applies an entry nobody else committed; 097 has the leader commit any entry a majority holds, whatever its term, which three terms verify in 25,666 states and the figure 8 configuration catches in sixteen steps, a leader of term 3 committing an entry of term 1 while the leader of term 4, elected without it, is about to overwrite it; 098 has a follower drop a conflicting previous entry the moment it refuses the request, proved safe under both configurations with six of the eight changed rows taken. The build tool gains the REPLICATION model entry (placed after the election model, so that role machine examples still match it), verify.sh runs the two contracts and the two configurations, and the spec, app, demo and root READMEs, the approaches table, the plugin README and the add-tla-model reference describe the model; two links broken by the previous cycle's edit in approaches.md and the plugin README are repaired. Verified by examples/demo/apps/quorum/verify.sh (55 tests, every contract, property and TLC configuration green) and by building 096 to 098 with examples/demo/tools/build.py, each with the verdict its example.json expects.

commits.summary: Check Raft log replication for liveness under fairness, a third configuration with three temporal properties, with three new examples
commits.body:
RaftReplication.tla gains fairness conditions (LiveSpec), written out with enabling predicates as the election model's are and one per leader and follower for Replicate, since fairness over the pair as a whole lets a leader starve a follower; three temporal properties for the runs that stay within the term budget: FollowersCatchUp (every entry in a leader's log reaches every follower), FollowersLearnCommits (no follower's commit index stays behind the leader's) and OwnEntriesAreCommitted (an entry a leader appends in its term is committed unless the leader is deposed); and EnablingAgrees. AdvanceCommit now asks the commit rule about any uncommitted entry, as figure 2 of the paper has it, rather than the first only, which never commits a log that starts with an earlier term's entry. Two configurations: RaftReplicationLive.cfg (three terms and one entry per leader, no symmetry: 14,388 states in about a minute; three terms because a run within the budget needs the leaders of two, one entry because a second multiplies the states by eight and the build runs TLC on one worker with coverage) and RaftReplicationEnabled.cfg (the predicates against ENABLED, 2,559 states in about ten minutes). The property that all commit indices agree was tried first and is false of the model: a server elected after a commit it had not heard of, with no entry of its own term, stays behind its followers for good, the paper's reason for the no-op entry a leader appends on taking office, which the model leaves out and the README now says.

Examples 099 to 101, all changes to AppendRule#decide: 099 leaves the commit index alone on a heartbeat (both safety configurations verify it; the fairness one reports FollowersLearnCommits violated by an eight-step run that stutters forever, the followers that appended before the commit never applying the entry); 100 refuses to overwrite a conflicting entry (safety verified; FollowersCatchUp violated by an eleven-step run that stutters forever, the leader at the start of the follower's log with nowhere to back up to, sending the same entry forever); 101 takes the commit index only on the heartbeat after an entry (verified under all three, 21,551, 9,269 and 14,958 states, both changed rows taken under each). Examples 096 to 098 are rebuilt under the third configuration and their texts updated (096 fails LeaderCompleteness under it in thirteen steps as well, 097 and 098 verify; the base configuration now has 20,253 states). build.py's REPLICATION entry gains the configuration and the three properties; verify.sh, the app and spec READMEs, the demo, root, examples and plugin READMEs, approaches.md and the add-tla-model skill reference are updated. Verified by examples/demo/apps/quorum/verify.sh (55 tests, every TLC configuration green, 13 minutes) and by build.py on 096 to 101, every verdict as expected. A lesson recorded in the skill reference: an enabling predicate that holds where its action cannot step makes the fairness condition unsatisfiable and the liveness check passes with nothing checked; a model that never commits passed OwnEntriesAreCommitted until its predicate was disabled too, which is what the Enabled configuration is for.

commits.summary: Generate the leader's reply rule into the Raft replication model as a third operator and let replies arrive late, twice or never under a fourth configuration, with three new examples
commits.body:
ReplyRule#decide is a new Quorum kernel: what a Raft leader does with a follower's reply to an AppendEntries request (RequestStatus AWAITED or ANSWERED, AppendReply accepted or refused; ADVANCE, BACK_UP or unchanged), with its behavioural contract and ReplyRuleContract.tla generated from it. RaftReplication.tla now runs the leader's half of the RPC through that operator (RequestNext, ReplyNext, Standing: an acceptance is news past the match index, a refusal only for the request at the next index past the match index, as etcd's progress tracker has it), and gains a DelayedReplies constant, a replies set, and the actions Ask and Answer, under which a reply waits on the wire, is handed to the leader twice, or never, and a leader asks again whether or not a reply is outstanding. RaftReplicationDelayed.cfg (two terms, one entry, 261,060 states) checks that with two invariants of the leader's record, MatchIndexIsRight and NextIndexPastMatch, which the one-step configurations leave out so that a wrong rule is still reported as the paper's property. Each action's guard is now an operator its enabling predicate shares, and the ENABLED comparison drops Replicate, whose nested record TLC evaluates thirty times slower under ENABLED and whose predicate restates its definition.

Examples 102 to 104, on ReplyRule: a leader that moves a follower up on a refusal records entries the follower lacks, and the first configuration finds leader completeness broken in twelve steps (a leader counting a follower that refused toward the majority that commits an entry the next leader overwrites); a leader that backs up on a refusal it has moved on from is verified by the three one-step configurations, which never hand the rule such a refusal, and the delayed one finds its record contradicting itself in twelve steps; a leader that takes a late acceptance as news moves a follower back and is proved safe under all four. Examples 096 to 101 were rebuilt under the fourth configuration, which verifies each of them, and their texts say why. jvmcontract tlc now honours JVMCONTRACT_JAVA_OPTS, since TLC's coverage mode fails at once with out-of-memory at Java's default heap on this model, and build.py sets -Xmx2500m for every TLC run. Verified by the quorum verify script (58 tests, every contract and property, 20 TLC configurations including the five of the replication model, the enabling check about four minutes with two workers), by the build of the nine examples, and by module-level mutation runs before the Java was written.

commits.summary: Add a verification pipeline: proofs and model checks queued as committed jobs and run asynchronously under resource limits
commits.body:
Development agents ran JBMC, TLC and build.py inline, which held them up for minutes at a time and let two sessions exhaust the machine together. Now an agent describes the verification a change needs as a job (verification/jobs/ID.json: title, description, capabilities, links, expectation, a rough estimate of CPUs, memory and duration, bash steps, and the files to bring back), commits it with the change marked (verification pending), and carries on. verification/pipeline.py submit writes jobs, and --example ID fills one in for a demo example.

pipeline.py run takes jobs from the latest commit, never the working copy, and runs each in a git archive of the commit that committed it. It runs several at once within a budget of workers, CPUs and memory, in priority order, and defers a job bigger than the runner allows rather than run it. Each step gets a systemd user scope with a hard MemoryMax (no swap), OOMPolicy=continue and a CPUQuota, and a timeout. JBMC's own limit and TLC's heap are set to fit inside the cap, and the scope's peak memory, CPU time, throttling and OOM kills are read from its cgroup before it goes away. A job that requires jvmcontract gets one built from lib/ at its commit, cached by the tree id of lib/. Results stay in an ignored state directory until pipeline.py collect brings them into verification/results/ID/ and applies the outputs of jobs that passed, unless a file changed since the job's commit, so another session's commit cannot sweep them up half-done. Each result records status, a one-line summary, what needs attention in words, every step's exit, time, memory and verdict lines from the log (JBMC, TLC, jvmcontract, build.py, cargo test, out-of-memory), the environment and tool versions, logs cut to head and tail past 2 MB, and a diff of the outputs. pipeline.py report gives a batch digest in Markdown or JSON, with the ones needing attention first and estimates compared with use per capability. resubmit reruns a job with other resources. The job and result formats are JSON schemas in verification/schema/. Configuration is pipeline.toml, a local override, and flags. Isolation is systemd or none, and the backend setting is the hook for a cloud runner, described in the README.

verification/README.md documents the lifecycle, submitting, estimates, reading results and the runner. The /run-verification skill is the procedure for the agent that manages the pipeline, including committing results without sweeping in another session's files. CLAUDE.md tells development agents to queue proofs instead of running them. build.py gains --index-only, so collecting several examples regenerates the examples table once.

Verified by verification/test_pipeline.py, 15 tests in throwaway git repositories, all passing. Covered: submit and validation, uncommitted jobs not run, outputs and verdict lines brought back, a failing step skipping the rest with its outputs kept and not applied, expected failure codes, timeouts, deferral and a bigger budget, jobs running side by side and one at a time, an output changed since the job's commit not overwritten, long logs cut with verdicts read from the whole log, resubmit, missing tools, a runner stopped mid-job leaving the job to run again, and under systemd an out-of-memory kill at a 100 MB cap and cgroup measurements. End to end, in a scratch clone: examples 076 (D1, TLC) and 052 (B11, JBMC) were submitted, run under systemd with jvmcontract built by the runner (63 s, 1.1 GB peak), and both gave their expected verdicts (12 s and 36 s, about 125 MB each). They were collected, with the examples table regenerated, and reported. The 1-CPU quota held the TLC step back 13.5 s, so the README now advises 2 CPUs for JVM work, and results flag heavy throttling. The pipeline has not yet run a real queue from a development session.
